strategies.summary: The NCU profile shows 122 registers/thread capping occupancy to 2 warps/SM (register-limited). The fused kernel's two-pass logsumexp with an unrolled C-channel loop over the full out_channels (e.g. 16) holds all partial sums in registers. Rewrite the logsumexp reduction to use a single-pass online algorithm (Welford-style max+sum combined) and restrict #pragma unroll to small, compile-time-bounded values. Add __launch_bounds__ to cap register allocation explicitly, targeting 64 registers/thread to allow occupancy of 4+ warps/SM.
implementation_hints: Add __launch_bounds__(256, 4) to the kernel signature to give nvcc a target occupancy hint and constrain register allocation.

Replace the two-pass logsumexp (separate max pass + sum-exp pass) with a single online pass: maintain running max_val and a corrected sum_exp that adjusts via exp(old_max - new_max) each time max_val increases. This eliminates re-reading the channel axis and halves live values.
Change #pragma unroll 16 to #pragma unroll 4 or remove unroll entirely on the channel loop; large forced unrolls are the primary register-pressure driver at runtime.
Keep the bias scalar extraction (item<float>()) outside the kernel call but pass it as a float argument â already done; confirm no extra tensor captures are live inside the kernel.
After the kernel rewrite, verify with a small correctness test: logsumexp over a known tensor must match torch.logsumexp to within 1e-5.
strategies.expected_gain: Doubling occupancy from 2 to 4 warps/SM should allow the scheduler to hide the remaining long-scoreboard stalls (currently 0.71 ratio) more effectively. Expect 20â40% reduction in fused kernel time; the conv dominates total time so net end-to-end gain is more modest (~5â15%).
risk_notes: Online logsumexp is numerically equivalent but must be validated carefully; a buggy max-correction term will silently produce wrong outputs.

__launch_bounds__ hints are advisory â if the kernel body still needs >64 registers nvcc will ignore the cap and spill to local memory instead, which would be slower. Validate register count in PTX/SASS.
out_channels=16 means the channel loop is short; unroll reduction benefits are limited and the register cost is high â removing unroll is very likely a net win here.
forbidden_patterns: two-pass logsumexp with separate max and sum loops at high unroll

review_notes.openai-compatible: Good risk-adjusted win for a register-limited kernel; online logsumexp and less unrolling directly target occupancy, but correctness must be validated.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Directly addresses the root bottleneck identified by NCU: 122 registers/thread capping occupancy at 2 warps/SM. Online logsumexp is a well-understood technique, removing large unroll factors is low-risk, and __launch_bounds__ gives the compiler a concrete target. Numerically equivalent if implemented correctly. Highest expected ROI of the portfolio.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Using a single-pass online logsumexp algorithm is a highly effective and standard way to reduce register pressure and memory bandwidth. Adding launch bounds is also a good practice for occupancy.

strategies.summary: With C=16 output channels after the transposed conv, the logsumexp reduction fits entirely within a single warp (16 values < 32 lanes). Restructure the kernel so that each warp collectively reduces one spatial position: lane 0..C-1 each load one channel value, then use warp shuffle intrinsics (__shfl_xor_sync / __shfl_down_sync) to compute the max and sum-exp entirely in registers without shared memory or global memory re-reads. This matches the problem shape (Câ¤32) perfectly and eliminates all L2 re-access for the reduction phase.
implementation_hints: Launch the kernel with blockDim = (32, 8) so each warp of 32 threads handles one spatial position collaboratively. Grid covers N * spatial_size / 8 blocks.

Inside the kernel, compute spatial_idx = blockIdx.x * 8 + (threadIdx.x / 32) and lane = threadIdx.x % 32. Each lane loads input channel = lane if lane < C, else -FLT_MAX (padding lanes to neutral values).

Use __shfl_xor_sync(0xffffffff, ...) tree reduction to find warp-wide max, then each lane computes exp(val - max) and a second shuffle-reduce sums the exponentials. Only lane 0 (or any designated lane) computes log(sum) + max and writes the output.
The bias subtraction and clamp can be inlined into the single writing lane with no extra memory traffic.
Use #pragma unroll on the warp shuffle tree since the reduction depth is fixed at ceil(log2(32))=5 steps.
strategies.expected_gain: Warp shuffle reductions have ~4-cycle latency versus ~30-cycle shared memory round-trips. Eliminating all shared memory usage for the reduction phase reduces smem pressure, potentially allowing more warps/SM. Combined with the register reduction from strategy 1, this could bring the fused kernel close to compute-bound behavior. Estimated 15â30% improvement in fused kernel time.
risk_notes: This restructuring changes the thread-to-work mapping fundamentally; the grid launch dimensions in the wrapper function must be updated to match.
Padding lanes (lane >= C) must load a neutral value (-FLT_MAX for max reduction, 0 for sum-exp) to avoid corrupting the reduction result.

If out_channels > 32, this approach requires a two-level reduction (multiple warps per spatial position) and becomes significantly more complex. Confirm C <= 32 at all expected model configs or add a fallback.
Warp divergence from the lane < C predicate is minimal (at most one partial warp boundary) but should be measured.
forbidden_patterns: per-thread full-channel sequential loop when warp-collective is applicable

review_notes.openai-compatible: Very promising if output channels stay <=32; warp-shuffle reduction fits the shape well and can remove shared-memory/global re-reads, with manageable risk if a fallback exists.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Warp shuffle reduction for C=16 is a clean fit: 16 values fit in a single warp, shuffle latency (~4 cycles) beats shared memory (~30 cycles), and the approach eliminates smem pressure entirely for the reduction phase. The restructured thread-to-work mapping and grid launch changes are non-trivial and the C<=32 constraint needs a runtime guard or static assert. Complements strategy_02 well; together they attack both the register pressure and the reduction latency.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Using warp shuffle intrinsics for the reduction when C=16 is an excellent, highly efficient approach that avoids shared memory overhead and maximizes register reuse.

strategies.summary: The fused kernel reads C channels per spatial element with stride=spatial_size between channels (NCDHW layout), producing non-coalesced strided global memory accesses. With 16 output channels and spatial sizes from a stride-2 conv, threads in a warp access different channel rows. Stage the channel data for each warp's batch of spatial positions into shared memory in a coalesced transposed load pattern (load NxC tile contiguously, then read per-element down the channel axis), eliminating the stride-C scatter pattern.
implementation_hints: Restructure the kernel so each block handles a tile of spatial positions (e.g., 256 positions) and all their C=16 channels. Allocate shared memory of shape [blockDim.x * C] floats.

In the load phase, each thread loads its own spatial position's full channel vector: thread i loads input[n * C * spatial_size + c * spatial_size + s] for c in 0..C-1. With C=16 this is 16 loads per thread, but they are now sequential in the thread's register file rather than strided warp-wide, making the warp-level access pattern C-channel-strided which is the current bottleneck.

Alternatively, use a cooperative tile load: assign each thread to load one (spatial_pos, channel) pair so that adjacent threads load adjacent memory locations (iterate over channels fastest). Store into smem[channel * blockDim.x + lane], then each thread reads smem[c * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x] for the reduction â fully coalesced global loads.
Use __ldg() (read-only cache) on the global load path if shared memory staging adds too much latency for small C.
Ensure smem bank conflict avoidance by padding shared memory rows: smem[(channel * (blockDim.x + 1)) + lane].
strategies.expected_gain: L2 throughput is currently at 91.8% of peak (severely L2-bound), and DRAM is only at 14.8%, indicating repeated L2 cache traffic from the strided access pattern. Coalescing the channel loads should reduce L2 transaction count and improve effective bandwidth utilization. Expected 10â25% improvement in fused kernel throughput.
risk_notes: Shared memory usage will increase per-block; with C=16 and blockDim=256, smem = 16*256*4 = 16KB which is within limits but reduces the SM's ability to run multiple blocks concurrently.
The cooperative load pattern requires all threads in the block to participate in the load barrier, adding synchronization overhead for small C. Benchmark against the simple per-thread approach.
Output channels C can vary at runtime based on model parameters â kernel must handle arbitrary C, not just 16.
forbidden_patterns: per-thread strided channel loop without coalescing
smem without bank-conflict padding when C is not a power of 2

review_notes.openai-compatible: Shared-memory staging for C=16 is likely overkill; added sync and smem pressure may offset the coalescing benefit.
review_notes.claude-compatible: The coalesced transposed-load pattern is the right idea but the numbers work against it here: 16KB smem per block with C=16 and blockDim=256 reduces SM block concurrency, and the synchronization barrier overhead for a small C may offset the coalescing gain. L2 at 91.8% peak suggests the access pattern matters, but strategy_02 (reducing register pressure to raise occupancy) is more likely to unlock latency hiding than adding smem staging. Worth trying after strategy_02 is validated.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Shared memory staging to coalesce strided global memory accesses is a strong technique, though it may introduce synchronization overhead and reduce occupancy if shared memory usage is too high.

strategies.summary: The NCU profile shows the dominant kernel is `convolveNd_dgrad_float_engine` â this is cuDNN's backward-data path being used for transposed convolution, not an optimized forward path. With stride=2, kernel=3, padding=1, and in_channels=3 to out_channels=16, the dgrad engine is suboptimal. Force cuDNN to select a different algorithm by using `torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True` in `__init__` or by explicitly converting the ConvTranspose3d weight to use `nn.functional.conv_transpose3d` with explicit `padding_mode` and algorithm selection. Alternatively, implement transposed convolution as explicit upsampling (insert_zeros stride-scattered input) + regular conv3d which may map to a more efficient cuDNN fprop kernel.
implementation_hints: In init_body, add `torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True` to enable autotuning; this alone may switch from dgrad_engine to a faster implicit GEMM variant on the first run.

Try replacing `nn.ConvTranspose3d` with an explicit `F.interpolate(x, scale_factor=stride, mode='nearest')` followed by `F.conv3d` with appropriate padding adjustments. For stride=2, kernel=3, this maps transposed conv to a standard conv on an upsampled input, which uses the fprop cuDNN path (typically faster than dgrad).

If using the upsample+conv approach: the effective weight for the forward conv must be rearranged (ConvTranspose3d weight axes are [in, out, kD, kH, kW] while Conv3d expects [out, in, kD, kH, kW]); transpose the weight in init, then register as a parameter.
Store the pre-permuted weight as `self.conv_weight` in init and call `F.conv3d` directly in forward to avoid repeated permutation.
Preserve padding semantics: ConvTranspose3d with stride=2, kernel=3, padding=1 produces output_size = (input_size - 1)*2 + 3 - 2 = 2*input_size. Verify output shape matches before replacing.
strategies.expected_gain: The dgrad engine runs at only 7.6% SM throughput and 30% warp occupancy. A properly tuned fprop path or implicit GEMM can reach 60â80% SM throughput for this problem shape. If the dominant kernel time drops by half, end-to-end speedup above the current 1.33x baseline could reach 1.8â2.2x.
risk_notes: Upsample+conv is mathematically equivalent only for integer strides and specific padding configurations. Edge outputs must be validated exactly.
cuDNN benchmark mode adds latency on the first forward pass (autotuning), which may penalize benchmarks that measure cold start.
Weight transposition must be done once in __init__ â doing it in forward() would add per-call overhead.
Groups parameter must be respected if non-trivial; the current init uses groups implicitly (default=1) but the forward call site must match.
forbidden_patterns: hardcoding output shape without verifying stride/padding math

review_notes.openai-compatible: Potentially large upside, but it is the riskiest option because equivalence, padding, and algorithm-selection behavior are easy to get wrong.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Targeting the correct dominant kernel (convolveNd_dgrad at 7.6% SM throughput) with a high-ceiling fix. Upsample+conv3d rerouting to the fprop cuDNN path is a meaningful architectural change with realistic 1.8-2.2x potential. Key risks are correctness of the weight axis permutation and padding math, both of which are verifiable. cudnn.benchmark cold-start penalty is a real concern for benchmarks. Strong strategy but requires careful validation.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Replacing ConvTranspose3d with upsample+conv3d is risky as it may not be mathematically equivalent for all padding/stride configurations. cuDNN benchmarking might also introduce unwanted cold-start latency.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import hashlib
from torch.utils.cpp_extension import load_inline

_STARK_EXTENSION = None

def _stark_strip_anchor_markers(source: str) -> str:
    cleaned_lines = []
    for line in source.splitlines():
        stripped = line.lstrip()
        if stripped.startswith('# <<<IMPROVE:') or stripped.startswith('# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>'):
            continue
        cleaned_lines.append(line)
    return '\n'.join(cleaned_lines)

def _stark_extension_name() -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha1((_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC) + _stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC)).encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()[:12]
    return f'stark_cuda_l2_p58_{digest}'

def _stark_get_extension():
    global _STARK_EXTENSION
    if _STARK_EXTENSION is None:
        _STARK_EXTENSION = load_inline(
            name=_stark_extension_name(),
            cpp_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC),
            cuda_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC),
            functions=None,
            extra_cflags=['-O3'],
            extra_cuda_cflags=['-O3', '--use_fast_math'],
            with_cuda=True,
            verbose=False,
        )
    return _STARK_EXTENSION

# <<<IMPROVE:user_helpers>>>
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

CUDA_CPP_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cpp>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>

// Add pybind exports for custom CUDA entrypoints here.
PYBIND11_MODULE(TORCH_EXTENSION_NAME, m) {}
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

CUDA_CU_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cu>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>
#include <cuda.h>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>

// Add CUDA kernels and exported wrapper functions here.
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

class ModelNew(nn.Module):
    """
        Model that performs a 3D transposed convolution, LogSumExp, HardSwish, subtraction, clamp operations.
        """
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride, padding, bias_shape):
        super().__init__()
        # <<<IMPROVE:init_body>>>
        self.conv_transpose = nn.ConvTranspose3d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride=stride, padding=padding)
        self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, 1, 1, 1))
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

    def forward(self, x):
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_1>>>
        # Baseline fallback keeps the official PyTorch forward path.
        # After implementing CUDA_CPP_SRC / CUDA_CU_SRC, call _stark_get_extension().your_entrypoint(...).
        x = self.conv_transpose(x)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_2>>>
        x = torch.logsumexp(x, dim=1, keepdim=True)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_3>>>
        x = x * torch.sigmoid(x + 3) / 6
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_4>>>
        x = x - self.bias
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_5>>>
        x = torch.clamp(x, min=-1, max=1)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_6>>>

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import hashlib
from torch.utils.cpp_extension import load_inline

_STARK_EXTENSION = None

def _stark_strip_anchor_markers(source: str) -> str:
    cleaned_lines = []
    for line in source.splitlines():
        stripped = line.lstrip()
        if stripped.startswith('# <<<IMPROVE:') or stripped.startswith('# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>'):
            continue
        cleaned_lines.append(line)
    return '\n'.join(cleaned_lines)

def _stark_extension_name() -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha1((_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC) + _stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC)).encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()[:12]
    return f'stark_cuda_l2_p58_{digest}'

def _stark_get_extension():
    global _STARK_EXTENSION
    if _STARK_EXTENSION is None:
        _STARK_EXTENSION = load_inline(
            name=_stark_extension_name(),
            cpp_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC),
            cuda_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC),
            functions=None,
            extra_cflags=['-O3'],
            extra_cuda_cflags=['-O3', '--use_fast_math'],
            with_cuda=True,
            verbose=False,
        )
    return _STARK_EXTENSION

# <<<IMPROVE:user_helpers>>>
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

CUDA_CPP_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cpp>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>

// Add pybind exports for custom CUDA entrypoints here.
PYBIND11_MODULE(TORCH_EXTENSION_NAME, m) {}
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

CUDA_CU_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cu>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>
#include <cuda.h>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>

// Add CUDA kernels and exported wrapper functions here.
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

class ModelNew(nn.Module):
    """
        Model that performs a 3D transposed convolution, LogSumExp, HardSwish, subtraction, clamp operations.
        """
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride, padding, bias_shape):
        super().__init__()
        # <<<IMPROVE:init_body>>>
        self.conv_transpose = nn.ConvTranspose3d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size, stride=stride, padding=padding)
        self.conv_transpose = self.conv_transpose.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last_3d)
        self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, 1, 1, 1))
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

    def forward(self, x):
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_1>>>
        if x.is_cuda:
            x = x.contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last_3d)
            x = self.conv_transpose(x)
        else:
            x = self.conv_transpose(x)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_2>>>
        x = torch.logsumexp(x, dim=1, keepdim=True)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_3>>>
        x = x * torch.sigmoid(x + 3) / 6
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_4>>>
        x = x - self.bias
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_5>>>
        x = torch.clamp(x, min=-1, max=1)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_6>>>
        return x
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
